## What it is

Thomas Kuhn described science as long periods of "normal science" broken by rare paradigm-shifting revolutions. Thinking about his own research, Gelman characterizes scientific progress as "self-similar (that is, fractal). Each level of abstraction, from local problem solving to big-picture science, features progress of the 'normal science' type, punctuated by occasional revolutions." The revolutions "have a fractal time scale, with small revolutions occurring fairly frequently (every few minutes for an exam-type problem, up to every few years or decades for a major scientific consensus)."

His examples run from the very large (from a magical to a scientific paradigm, or from behaviorism to cognitive psychology) to the very small. On a consulting problem, he writes, "I typically will start in a certain direction, then suddenly realize I was thinking about it wrong, then move forward," and that reevaluation "can happen several times in a couple of hours." His summary: "Scientific progress is fractal in size of problem and in time scale."

## Why it matters

The fractal view softens the sharp Kuhnian split between normal science and revolution. Your own work has revolutions: realizing you were thinking about a problem wrong is the same kind of event as a field changing its paradigm, only smaller and faster. Gelman ties this to his view of Bayesian data analysis: "deductive Bayesian inference as normal science and model checking as potentially revolutionary."

## How it works

Gelman's claim is qualitative: the same pattern of normal science punctuated by revolutions appears at every scale. He doesn't propose a particular statistical distribution for the sizes of revolutions.

**The simulation is our toy illustration, not part of his argument.** One standard way to make "self-similar across scales" concrete is a power law, $\Pr(\text{size} > s) \propto s^{-\alpha}$. On log-log axes its survival curve is a straight line, and the line keeps the same slope when you zoom into a smaller range and rescale. Whether real scientific change follows a power law is an open empirical question. The simulation only shows what scale-free self-similarity looks like.

## Simulated example

A **toy model**: hypothetical sizes of conceptual changes are drawn from a power law, one simple scale-free distribution. Plot the survival curve on log-log axes for all changes, and then for a "zoomed-in" view that only sees changes below some size, rescaled. The point is the shape (the same at every scale), not the specific distribution.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
import {rng, range, fmt} from "../js/stats.js"
```

```{ojs}
viewof alpha = Inputs.range([0.5, 2.5], {value: 1.2, step: 0.1, label: "Power-law exponent α"})
viewof seed = Inputs.range([1, 500], {value: 145, step: 1, label: "Random seed"})
```

```{ojs}
rev = {
  const r = rng(seed);
  const sizes = range(5000).map(() => Math.pow(1 - r(), -1 / alpha)).sort((a, b) => b - a);
  const ccdf = arr => arr.map((s, i) => ({s, p: (i + 1) / arr.length}));
  const sub = sizes.filter(s => s < 20);
  return [...ccdf(sizes).map(d => ({...d, view: "All of science"})), ...ccdf(sub.map(s => s * 5)).map(d => ({...d, view: "Zoomed into a subfield (rescaled)"}))];
}
```

```{ojs}
Plot.plot({
  ariaLabel: "Scientific revolutions: simulation chart",
  ariaDescription: "Horizontal axis: Size of the conceptual change (log scale). Vertical axis: Share of changes at least this big (log scale). The chart updates with the controls above it, and the summary below the charts states the result in words.",
  height: 300,
  x: {type: "log", label: "Size of the conceptual change (log scale)", grid: true},
  y: {type: "log", label: "Share of changes at least this big (log scale)", grid: true},
  color: {legend: true, range: ["#2166ac", "#d6604d"]},
  marks: [Plot.line(rev, {x: "s", y: "p", stroke: "view", strokeWidth: 2})]
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const all = rev.filter(d => d.view === "All of science");
  const big = all.filter(d => d.s > 100).length;
  return html`<div class="sim-readout">${md`In this toy model, both views fall along nearly straight lines on log-log axes, so the pattern looks the same at every scale. Of 5,000 simulated changes, **${big}** are more than 100 times the minimum size (the "Kuhnian revolutions"), with no gap separating them from the rest. This illustrates self-similarity. It isn't evidence about how real scientific change is distributed.`}</div>`;
}
```

## Key takeaways

::: takeaways
- Gelman sees the normal-science-and-revolution pattern at every scale, from minutes on a consulting problem to decades in a field.
- Realizing you were thinking about a problem wrong is a small revolution of the same kind as the famous ones.
- In his Bayesian view, inference within a model is normal science and model checking is potentially revolutionary.
:::
